utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. All the accused are here. Defence teams are all here with the exception of Ms. Condon who is sick. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. So good morning once more. There are a few matters that we'd like to address. Then after that we will continue with the exhibits process that we left -- we interrupted yesterday. And then after the first break, we'll hand down our decision on some of the issues that were raised yesterday, in particular, in relation to these exhibits, but also other matters. So you would be aware that yesterday the Prosecution filed a motion for protective measures for Witness number 86. You would be aware also that this witness is due to testify immediately after the next two. It's our decision to raise this matter now to see whether there is any response on the part of the Defence teams, whether there is any objection to the granting of these protective measures so that if there are none we can decide the same. Yes, I see that there are none. So the Trial Chamber is seized with the Prosecution motion for protective measures for Witness 86, filed on the 7th of March 2007. It makes reference to the details contained therein, and the request of the Prosecution to have in place protective measures of pseudonym and facial distortion. There being no objection and since the Trial Chamber is convinced of the -- considers this request justified, motion is granted. Then there is a confidential Prosecution motion for leave to convert one 92 bis intercept operator witness to 92 ter witness, which was filed on the 5th of March. This relates to Witness number 75, who is the next one, I understand, to give evidence. There are two issues that I would like to raise. The first one obviously is whether there is any objection from the Defence teams to the conversion of this witness to a 92 ter witness. And the second thing is more or less related first to the Prosecution, but we'll still need to know what the position of the Defence team is. You have not really asked for the continuation of the protective measures assigned to this witness in Blagojevic, or for new -- or for new protective measures to be put in place. I mean this has been verified because we do verify with each and every witness, especially those who have already testified in other proceedings. So let's start with the first one. Is there any objection on the part of any of the Defence teams to the conversion of this witness to a 92 ter? There are none. So that part of the motion -- that motion is granted. And I don't need to go into the details of the motion. It's a motion that was filed on the 5th of March. Do I take it also that you are requesting for the protective measures granted in Blagojevic to remain in place, or are you seeking additional protective measures for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning. Yes, we would request the -- the Blagojevic protections remain in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Are there any objections on the part of any of the Defence teams? We hear none. So the same protective measures will remain in place. Thank you. There is also a Prosecution motion which was filed three days ago on the 5th of March, for leave to supplement the 65 ter list of exhibits for two exhibits from Witness 154's prior testimony. This motion concerns Witness number 154, who will be not the next one, the one after, and who could actually start testifying today. Is there any objection on any of the Defence teams to have these two exhibits included in the 65 ter list? We hear none. So that motion is also granted. And again, I don't need to refer to the substance or to the relevant parts of the motion, it's granted in toto. Finally you will recall that in the course of last week I had, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, invited you to further your consultations, particularly Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Haynes, who had stood up to deal with this matter in relation to the confidential Prosecution submission or motion to convert 12 viva voce witnesses to 92 ter witnesses. I don't think I need to repeat what the substance of the debate was at the time. I had the undertaking of both sides that you will take your time to discuss this further and possibly come back with a solution to offer to the Trial Chamber, failing which we will proceed to decide the matter. Not today, obviously, because we are not prepared to give our decision today. So, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. On that issue, Mr. Haynes invited us for three witnesses to do viva voce. We agreed with him on one, and denied -- turned down his invitation on the other two. Given a moment, I can give you the witness number that we -- we agreed on, but of course it was all per -- you know, subject to your final ruling, but I -- we can -- I'm reminded by my colleague, it's 108 was the one that we...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We agreed to go viva voce with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 108, that is the witness number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had agreed also here in open court about Peccerelli, in other words, I had Mr. Haynes speaking, I assume, on behalf of everyone that there was no objection as far as Peccerelli was concerned. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The only two witnesses that we are left unagreed upon, if that's even a word, are, I think, 117 and 132. And to cut the matter short now, there is likely to be an issue you're going to have to decide there because, as I said to you when I introduced the discussion, there is a point of principle about this. And I can set that out briefly in writing during the course of today if you would like me to or we can argue it orally at some stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I would prefer to have -- I mean arguing it orally will take more of our court time, so if it's not much work for you, we would appreciate to have it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I will undertake to get something to you by the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you so much. If, however, any of these witnesses are due to testify Monday -- all right. Because in that case at least we would argue -- try to -- try to get some kind of feedback on that particular witness. But I see from the Prosecution side that that's not the case. So we may safely proceed. And I thank you so much, first, for your efforts, all of you, to try to reach this agreement. The Trial Chamber is always appreciative of this. And we will await your -- your filing, to which we will give you one day, Mr. McCloskey, then to respond. So that by Monday morning -- by Monday we would have -- we would be in a position to start discussing amongst ourselves. The last thing is, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Zivanovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may be seated, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have informally approached the Chamber, intimating that your client would like to be exempted from attending this Friday's sitting for reasons that you have very aptly described. We have considered that. You don't need to formalise it. However, we would like to have a written waiver signed by your client according to the procedure that is normal and to which you would be familiar. So otherwise, Mr. Popovic can stay away on Friday, provided we have this undertaking and waiver. All right. So I think we can safely start, and then we'll come back to you on the various issues that were raised yesterday by -- by some of you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one matter I wanted to raise that I hope will save us a little time. You were -- you are aware of the next witness and his testimony in the Blagojevic case. He basically speaks of two exhibits. One a notebook of intercept -- of tactical intercepts that was done by him in his little unit where he was near Nezuk, and one stack of papers of intercepts that was done by his unit down closer towards Srebrenica. In reviewing those materials, I have made the decision that the papers, the pile of papers, is not something I will be asking the Court to take any evidence or acts or conduct of any accused on. There are some vague references that could be considered acts or conduct, but given the -- just it's unnecessary for the Prosecution to take that evidence in that way. I will not be offering any acts or conduct evidence from that material, and as you know, my burden for the acts of conduct evidence is greater, pursuant to your -- your ruling. So I have told that to Defence counsel, and those papers are here and are part of the former record, and available for the Court, but I am not asking any acts or conduct evidence from any of that material. As for the notebook for the other material, that principally goes to the acts or conduct of -- of General Pandurevic, which Mr. Haynes and I will be debating perhaps some issues, but you will see how that folds out. But that's just the background of -- I am not aware of any other acts or conduct in that material from other accused, though there are lots of code-names that I am not at this time aware of who they are. That may pop up later on, but I don't think so. So at this point, just for your knowledge, the notebook will go to acts or conducts of General Pandurevic. Also, and I'm sure you are aware of this, there will be witnesses in the future that will be speaking directly to these intercepts, people that were actually involved in these intercepts as a participant or overheard them. That's true of both these tacticals, as well as the others. But having said that, I don't think we need to wait until the end for you to make any ruling on these intercepts, but just as you -- as you see these tacticals, I -- there will be other evidence about them, because they are, as I said before, a bit of a different animal, as you will see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you know, we handed down an order yesterday in relation to intercepts. We think it is of the utmost importance for the Defence teams in particular to know what our position is in relation to intercepts, because I can't -- we are -- we strongly feel that no Defence team should be put in a position where they have to start their defence without knowing exactly where they stand in relation to intercepts. So irrespective of when you plan to bring forward these witnesses, we will be proceeding with the exercise that we intimated we will be -- one thing, Mr. McCloskey. I mean -- and can I refer you to line 11 of page 6, please? I will not read it again. There is the mention of a place there where this next witness was supposed to be working. Do you wish to redact that or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I -- I used the term "near" because it's actually another place. And I thought that that would be okay in this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a difficult issue. I -- I have edited another -- I edited my summary a bit because yesterday we had people in the audience, and I will read again that edited version to try to make it the safest possible. In fact, I've referred to the -- can we go into private session for just one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr, Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Mr. President, you just made reference to the order that issued by the Trial Chamber concerning the intercept evidence. And there is one issue I'd like to bring. I don't know if this is the proper time or not, but in the order issued by the Trial Chamber at paragraph 1, the Prosecution is being asked to file a written submission highlighting the prima facie relevance of each tendered intercepted communication. We feel, and of course I speak for this team only at this time, not having consulted with my colleagues yet, we feel that this is very important indeed, that the Prosecution gives the prima facie relevance of each intercept and that they go further than saying this intercept is relevant to all counts in the indictment. This will greatly facilitate our position in order to be able -- for us to answer and respond and then get meaningful debate out of this intercept issue. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we understand the order and look forward to meeting it in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And then if it's not satisfactory to any of the Defence teams, of course we will be prepared to hear any submissions, to receive any submissions that you may have. So let me go back one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were about to -- we had finished with your list, of course with the caveat that we would be deciding on the remaining issue, and then we were supposed to deal with the other request to tender documents. I think we should start with you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't know. I mean, Mr. Bourgon, I got the impression yesterday that you had finished with the tendering process. Or do you have -- do you have anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. When the session closed yesterday, I was absent, but my colleague raised the issue. The issue that was being debated was whether the statement P2463 should be admitted in evidence. And debate closed where we ran out of time and we did not get a chance to fully argue the matter. And our position is that the statement can go into evidence, but not the date report which accompanied that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic did deal with that in your absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It is because in the transcript it's not -- the matter wasn't completed and then we stopped the hearing yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to hear more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is any new submission you would like to make, yes, go ahead. But I think we've heard enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, the -- based on yesterday's transcript, there was the issue of the statement. And we oppose the fact that the date report should not accompany that statement. But then I take it that my -- I'm not sure if my colleague was finished with his list and whether he wanted to get into evidence the -- the report on the equipment, whether he was going to submit a request for the report on the equipment, which is another thing that we also want to oppose if my colleague wants to put that order for the equipment in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. But I think Mr. Vanderpuye yesterday was quite clear that he was not including this -- or that document in the list of documents he wished to tender, the Prosecution wished to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that matter is moot. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're tendering no exhibits, Your Honour, with respect to the last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Does any other of the Defence teams wish to tender exhibits? Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, document 5D198, that must remain under seal because it reveals the name of the witness and for the time being is not yet translated into English, we only have the B/C/S version for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also made use of 199. Do you wish to tender that as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from the Prosecution or from any of the other Defence teams? Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. No, we don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So this is being admitted, marked for identification purposes, pending the finalisation of the translation process. All right. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry to come back on the issue of this date book, which comes from another witness, but there is, as was made clear before the Trial Chamber yesterday, the full date book was shown to us at the break, just before we completed our cross-examinations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We would like this date book to be disclosed to us and we believe that it includes some information that would be very important for our case. Moreover, there is a possibility that we will ask for further cross-examination of the witness who -- to whom this book belongs, which was a witness that testified here and that never made reference to this book at that time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll come to that when we are seized with the matter, and in the meantime, Mr. McCloskey, do you wish to indicate whether you are disclosing that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That book was provided to them yesterday to get a good look at it. Ms. Nikolic asked me this morning if we could get a copy of it and we're seeing if we can do that before it flies away. But I'm sure we'll be able to work that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So any further preliminary matters that you would like to discuss or to debate? None. So I think we can bring in Witness number 75. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before the witness starts, don't put his earphones on for the time being. Ask him to sit down. Please make yourself comfortable. There is one further issue that I forgot to mention when I was dealing with this witness. Even though you referred to the subject matter thereof. You referred during your intervention to the tactical intercept notebooks. These documents were, if you go back to our decision of the 12th September of last year, we had marked these for identification purposes. This was our decision on Rule 92 bis statements. We have tried to match these documents with your 65 ter list of exhibits, which you submitted earlier on that year, on the 28th of April. And we may be wrong, we stand to be corrected, I mean we make mistakes every day, like you -- like the rest of us. But if they are not, and please check, you will need to address this in order to conform with the procedure that we have established. Unless there is no objection on the part of the Defence teams, and we can then proceed. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I have a number. I think it's correct, but we'll check on it to make sure that that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry to be so finicky, but I think we need to be. So, good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. Before you start giving evidence, Madam Usher is going to hand you a piece of paper, that contains the text of a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth which you are required to make before you start your testimony. So please stand up, read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. We have put in place for you two protective measures, namely the use of a pseudonym. You will be referred to as -- by a number rather than by your name. And also we are distorting the image of your face, so no one can recognise you. Is that to your satisfaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. McCloskey will go first, and he will then be followed by the members of the Defence teams. Mr. McCloskey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. If you could first take a look at this paper which we parked P02464 and tell us, is that you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you recently had a chance to hear your testimony from a previous trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was it correct, to the best of your knowledge and memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if you were asked those same questions again, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to read a brief summary of that testimony, pursuant to the system I've told you about. The witness was born in Bosnia and Herzegovina and grew up in a town near Sapna in Eastern Bosnia. He went to secondary school and graduated in the field of electronics. In 1989 he did his mandatory service with the JNA and was trained as a radio telegraph operator. When the war broke out in 1992 he joined the Territorial Defence and worked in communications jobs, repairing and maintaining communications equipment. As the war continued he worked as a member of the BiH and was involved in monitoring and intercepting radio communications. Could we go into private session for the next couple of paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The enemy frequencies were scanned, and when a frequency was found containing communication, an operator from his unit would transcribe in summary fashion the intercepted conversation on a piece of paper, as it was occurring. The conversation was not written down verbatim. The operator would write quickly to keep up with the conversation and use abbreviations to assist in the process. The conversations were not tape-recorded in July 1995. The operator would give the paper with the conversation on it to the witness and he would pass the information on up the chain via military telephone. At the end of the day, most of the conversations from the pieces of paper were copied into a notebook by one of the operators and the paper was normally destroyed. The witness kept one notebook containing intercepted conversations from the period around the fall of Srebrenica enclave, which was used in the site one location. And a stack of notes of conversations from the site two location. The piece of paper from site two were pieces of paper that the operators transcribed the conversations on. The witness was asked to comment on an intercept from the notebook from site one on page 7 of the English translation from 14 July, ERN number 0084-8952 from the original B/C/S text. The witness said he remembered this conversation because it was inconceivable to him that a road was being built at this time during the war. The witness identified the handwriting of one of his -- of one of the operators and named that operator. After the war, the witness attempted to provide the notebook and the notes mentioned in his testimony to the BiH for archiving purposes, but the documents were not accepted by the BiH soldiers doing the archival work. Based on a request several years ago from the OTP, the witness searched for other tactical intercept records, but was unable to find any remaining records. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you, when you were working in July, did you have a military rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's redact these last few words. Go into private session straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would just now like to ask you a few questions about what I referred to in the summary as this notebook that was taken from site one. And I'd like to give you the -- the original notebook, if I could, and there's some little stickies on here that will help -- help you get referenced. And if we, on the ELMO -- sorry, not -- if we could put that on the ELMO, and I've showed you how to try to work the ELMO and the microphone, and if we could get the -- well, actually, I think we'll just work from the B/C/S at this point, is probably simpler. So if you could -- if we could -- first of all, let me ask you. I think it was back in 1999, did the Prosecution contact you and ask you to review that material to see if there was anything relevant to Srebrenica that you could think of or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you go through your notebook and mark in red pen three items in response to that request?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when the Prosecution saw that you had marked the notebook in red pen, what did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, I told them that I marked the conversations, and then I was told that I shouldn't have done it, but it was too late. It was already done. There was no going back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So can we -- we've got those three markings. If we could just put that on the ELMO, and we've marked the first one with number 1. And if we could get that on the ELMO and you could just tell us briefly, read out what you have marked. And the ELMO is very sick, you can't see the colour there unfortunately, Mr. President. But could you point with your finger where the red mark is that you had made on the book, just on the book itself so everyone can see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this particular -- this is P02231. Okay. And so why did you mark that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, this frequency has to do with the work of police forces of the Zvornik MUP. Based on the conversation one could tell that they were recruiting people for the field. They were ordered to stand under full military equipment. That was on the 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Just preceding the operations in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And let's go to number 2, which is also marked. And perhaps I should read the ERN number of that page. The ERN, as we can see is 0084-8947. And we see -- we actually can see the red mark this time. Can you tell us -- we see a date, I believe, of 12 July. What is this, and why did you mark it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Once again, this is the frequency of the Zvornik MUP. They are mentioning full military equipment once again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last bit of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, the interpreters didn't hear the last bit of your reply. If you could kindly repeat it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the frequency of the Zvornik MUP, once again. Once again they are speaking of recruitment and full military equipment and then a name is mentioned, and the name is underlined in red.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the third one that you have marked. And this is 0084-8952. We see some red, I hope you can see those red dots and a little red arrow. Can you again -- now, can you -- and if I could, could we have on the e-court, it should be P02232, page 7. So we can see the English of this. And while we're waiting for that, can you read the part that you had marked for -- for the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: "Maric, Miladinovic, Mitrovic, member of the engineering corps, they should stand by Rijeska with excavators in order to pave the road."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I know that's a bit unfair to do that to the interpreters but if I could read the official English translation just for the record. Unfortunately it hadn't come up yet. Page 7 of that document, please. I don't know what page that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you can proceed by reading while this is -- yeah, okay it is there now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As we can see in the English it says, "For Maric, Miladinovic, Mitrovic (engineers) to come at Nedo's inn with the excavator in order to widen the road."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, why did you note that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: It seemed suspicious to me that somebody could work on creating a road, paving a road simultaneously with all these combat operations going on. So I remember -- I remember this conversation, even today. We immediately assumed that this could not have been anything to do with the road, that it must involve something else. And later on it turned out that we were right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us, just by reference, I think we can go back to what has been marked with a yellow number 1 in your book, it's actually page 4 of the English, and note the date that this information was taken on. It's number 1 on the yellow sheet, and it's page 4 on the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You can lead on the date. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 14 July, is -- is the date that's noted in the book. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to number 3 in the yellow page of the original book, which is page 8 in the e-court. And this is just basically the beginning date that shows 15 July. And if we could, after showing which date we're talking about, now go to -- to page 13 on the e-court, and page 4 on the original. And I want to read a section and ask you a bit about it. And it says -- I'm reading the part where it starts, "Vuk-Ikar-Pavle- I talked to Semso (Vuk) and stopped the activities. They care for the head of column (soldiers). I suggested him to release all those from the central prison in Tuzla and we would release these. Pavle-we don't have a mandate to negotiate." The next page on the English, page 14. "What did Semso say about the captured policemen. He says that they are alive. If something happened to them, all others will be finished. It will be 100 for one. And after that he fired three more rounds (Rogatica). Pavle told him not to negotiate with him. We'll kill them in the woods. And he can fire at Serbia, Belgrade, Zvornik as much as he wants. Tell him that all of them should surrender in Orahovac." Now, we know from your testimony that you've described these as being written in a summary fashion. But when I wrote like this my grammar teacher said this was full of indefinite references. Can you put this into context for us, who is talking about who? Because if it's summary form, it's -- unless you were doing it, it's difficult to tell. For example, "I talked to Semso and stopped the activities." Is that a direct quote, is that -- can you -- can you just fill us in on that a bit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: This is a member of the army of Republika Srpska who spoke with Semso, and Semso wanted to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How could you tell that Semso wanted to negotiate from this text?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, he says, "I spoke to Semso," the VRS member talked to Semso and says that Semso would like to talk to him and that he asked the Turks' frequency. I actually remember that myself. That the frequency was requested from people who were at the head of the column that was breaking through out of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From this bit, can -- is the operator hearing anything from Semso, or just from the Serb person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Only the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So it's fair to say that this -- this information is being said by -- can you tell how many participants are saying this? Is this one person that is saying what I just read or is it more than one Serb soldier or officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: There were two, because you always need to have two speakers. In this case it was Vuk Lovac and in the continuation of the conversation you can see that they continue to speak about this conversation with Semso, because it is mentioned that a member of the army of Republika Srpska asked for people to be released from the central prison and then this one later told him, also a member of the army of Republika Srpska, that he was not authorised to negotiate and that Semso can say whatever he wants. But that they are going to kill those people in the woods. There was no question of negotiations or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's -- is there any way, from your records, to sort out, from this book, to sort out any sort of time-frame for this communication, when that occurred on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: 1330 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: The time is written down, Vuk Lovac, 1330 hours and then there is the next part of the conversation at 1300 hours 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, I see. That is in the section before the one I started to read. Okay. So that up at 1330, is that where the conversation actually started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes, that's when it started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's go from the afternoon of the 15th now to the page that begins with 16 July. It's number 15 in e-court, it's number 5 on your little yellow sheet. He can probably flip it himself, but...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't mean to be difficult, but the only person who's got the yellow stickies is the witness and it would be helpful if we could have the B/C/S e-court references so that the accused could make proper comparison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I fully agree and I thank you for pointing that out, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's 18, and when we get to it, I can read the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, until just -- are you working on it, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: B/C/S e-court is 18, but he's flipping to it in the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The original document in B/C/S is on the ELMO, so everyone following B/C/S can follow on the ELMO, and then the English version is in e-court, in the English channel. Maybe for reference the Prosecution can give the page number in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that satisfactory, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the theory, if I can see on the ELMO, we can get the ERN I can just repeat it for the record. If it's 0084-8958. But that's just to orient us to the 16, if we could now turn the pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Each time refer specifically to the page, Mr. McCloskey, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We -- on the English version is 16, which should be on e-court. And the -- it's number 6 of the yellow tab on the original. Which is on the B/C/S e-court, 18. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what I wanted to refer you to is an entry that says 1330 hours, "Their evacuation is going to start. If they shoot you shoot as well. Users covered the area from our/unintelligible/and homed in artillery. They were not audible. They work with small power." Can you tell us again, "Their evacuation is going to start." Who is that -- who is speaking now, or which side is speaking and who is the "they" referred to, based on your knowledge of how this worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: The specific conversation says, "Their evacuation will begin." They are thinking of the evacuation of the Muslims. And this is spoken by a member of the army of Republika Srpska. If they fire, if the Muslims fire, then you should fire too. He is giving him some sort of approval, or permission, that if anybody from the Muslim side shoots, that they should then fire in return. And at the end of the conversation it says that the participants worked with small strength. This is not understood. It means that we were not able to pick up the rest of the conversation because it was fading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just the -- my last little section is marked on tab 7 in the original, and we can see that's just the next ERN, I believe. Yes, last digits 8962. It's page 19 in the English e-court, and I want to take you down to the bottom of the English version, it -- and in the B/C/S it -- the part I wanted to ask you about says, "Palma in person for Lovac 1 in person. We are negotiating with the opposing side that they get out in the direction of Nezuk. Down the stream and up to the left towards Zuta/zemlja/yellow soil/." Again can you tell us which side -- which side is talking. Just orient us a bit on this? When it says "we," who is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Members of the army of Republika Srpska. They are saying that they had agreed with our side, the Muslim side. That a number of the Muslims could get out in the direction of Nezuk, and they are giving the route of movement to the left towards Zuta/zemlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you, from looking at your notebook, give us any idea of roughly the time or precisely the time, whatever, that this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: The exact time is not given here, but it was after 12.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's -- let me continue, which is the next page in the English, page 20 may be the same page on the B/C/S, and it starts off -- B/C/S e-court 20, page 23, "Palma-Lovac 1-we agreed that their access is going to be towards the stream so that we liberate Resnik and Govedarica." Again, the "we" is who or what side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: These are members of the army of Republika Srpska who are speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So that is the same for the next line. "We are going to open it there and once it passes we are returning to our old positions. It is about the withdrawal of our dead and wounded and the Chetniks received an order to shoot if someone attempted to go into the depth of the territory." Now, again, let's try to be clear on this. "We are going to open it there and once it passes we are returning to our old positions." Who is the "we" in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Members of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And now we have this statement, "It is about the withdrawal of our dead and wounded." Do you know who the "our dead and wounded" are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: They were members of the army of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then it says, "And the Chetniks received an order to shoot." So I don't imagine the Serb forces are referring to themselves as Chetniks, are they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: This was the operator's note, or remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I think you probably testified about this, but just one last question. You have testified that you worked in -- with the operators. How is it that you are able to tell who is speaking and help us understand that? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I spent a lot of time myself in such centres during the war, before the fall of Srebrenica, and before all these activities around Srebrenica. So a large number of these conversations I am familiar with. As for the remarks or notes by the operators, they used to do that often. It didn't have the form of a report. Often next to the authentic text the conversation would be summarised and then in the context of that you would say "they" meaning the army of Republika Srpska and when you say "we" or "us" they meant the army of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last question in private session, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that you testified in another case before this Tribunal, and of course you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I saw that in that case you said that these notebooks -- you handed the notebooks from what you can remember, you gave them up to Ms. Stefanie, you didn't mention her last name. So what would I like to ask you is if you remember exactly whom -- to whom you handed over the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I just managed to remember Stefanie, that name. She was in that team. So I handed over the notebooks to her, to Stefanie. She was the first one of the team that I met.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you handed over the notebooks, did you make a document, did you sign anything, did you sign anything, did she sign anything or someone else, did they sign anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: No, I didn't sign anything. I have no documents relating to that and I cannot remember if there was anything like that on the part of the Prosecutor. If it was some document with some kind of protocol number, I probably would have asked to have this document to cover myself, but since it was just a notebook, I didn't have any special measures about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember approximately when you handed over the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 1999. You told us, amongst other things, that the documents that were at location one and location two, as we're calling it here, that you tried to hand over the documents to the archivists of your unit, of your command, and that they refused to accept that. Can you tell us what their reasons were, why they refused to accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: The only and the main reason was that the notebook was not in the form of a report, it didn't have a protocol number. Because based on a protocol number, you could make some kind of document to enter the notebook into the archive. So it had nothing to do with the content of the notebook, it was just the fact that it wasn't registered properly, paginated and so on. They didn't even want to look at what was inside the notebook, at the material contained in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And because of that, did you address any of your superiors, did you point out the problem that the archive personnel did not want to accept into the archives that material that was of exceptional importance? How was that resolved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: It was very difficult to resolve that because, in the command system, there was an order and it's very clear in that order what is archived and what is not. I tried to go around that, but it didn't work. So I returned the notebook to my safe, and I kept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the information that we have here, you had your first contact with the Prosecution on the 17th of May, 1999, and that was when you talked about what your work was. In the document that is called an information report here, it is stated that the witness is sure that many conversations were registered and stored in the archives. Can you please -- that many of the conversations were written down and are archived. Do you recall that in your contact with a certain Alastair Graham?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said, and it was true. But not -- does not refer to the notebooks in location one, it refers to notebooks from location two. Those conversations were properly archived. Unfortunately, I didn't manage to find them later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before you testified the last time before the Tribunal, you had some notes that you had in preparation for your testimony, and we received those notes. They are your conversations with investigators and members of the OTP. And at that time, in the conversation, you mentioned the documentation from those two locations, but you said that the documents were not received into the archives, either from location one or from location two. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: It's not the entire archive, it's probably the part that you have in the other notebooks from the other centre, which we indicated to be location two. So you do have some material from there that they also did not wish to accept, together with this other notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell me, what was accepted into the archive and wasn't found later, what exactly was that? Were they papers or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: They were reports. Reports that were forwarded to the division command in the encrypted form, and they were also at the command from Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say Kladanj, it's neither one of those centres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but it was sent through the encryption section via Paket radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In 2002 you had another interview with the OTP investigators, with a certain Jean Gagnon, and on that occasion you said that you were going to get in touch with one of your colleagues who also worked on that with you. I'm not going to mention his name, but I assume that you know who I'm referring to. And that you were going to ask him if he still had the intercepts from that period. My question is, since you had these notebooks that you talked about and in view of the fact that some of them were presented to the archives through the reports, you expected that your colleague would also have some intercepts from that period. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I didn't accept -- I didn't expect that I wasn't completely convinced, but I sort of had it in the back of my mind that perhaps he had the original notes, because from location one, the transcripts or the conversations were copied later, or parts of it. So I assume that perhaps he did have some of the original papers, because he was there for a lot of the time; although, most of those papers were destroyed and actually he confirmed that most of the papers were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's time to have the break a few minutes ahead. 25 minutes. Is that sufficient because of the redactions? 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As we stated earlier on at the beginning of the sitting we are going, before we continue with the evidence of the witness -- should do it after. Okay. Let's leave it until later. Let's continue with the evidence, and then we'll hand down the decision later on after we are finished with his testimony. Mr. Zivanovic has finished his cross-examination. Who is going next? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to have a couple questions for you, and very few maybe with 20 minutes, I think we should be able to finish, hopefully. You mentioned this morning on page 31 in your answer to my learned colleague of the Defence on lines 21 and 23 that you turned over your book to a woman with the Prosecution named Stefanie. And what I'd like to first confirm that, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I know that I talked to Stefanie, but I can't remember exactly whether she was the one, it's been quite a long time since then, so I can't remember. I think that it was Stefanie. She was the first one that I talked to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To help refresh your recollection, I'm going to give you her last name and you could tell me if that helps refresh your recollection. I have in our notes and records, a woman who worked for the Office of the Prosecutor at or around that time by the name of Stefanie Frease. Does that help refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the last name. There was a Stefanie from the Prosecution, yes. There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in your book that you brought with us that we have seen the original, there is a lot of code-names listed, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any time did you try to decipher the code-names that were identified in your book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, at that time while this was being done I wasn't really interested in it much, the actual name of the participants. I was more interested in learning the facts and how the facts could be used to promote the interests of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In radio communication it is quite difficult to learn the actual name of participants. One can make some conclusions based on commands, headquarters, and so on, maybe some other factors are important, but you can learn more about the rank and function than learn the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just briefly show you Exhibit 1084, which was previously introduced in the record. And it's going to appear hopefully on the screen in front of you. And these are VRS code-names that were prepared, I believe, and I say it respectfully, prepared by the Office of the Prosecution and Ms. Frease or her group at that time. When you get it up, I'll ask you a question, Mr. Witness. Okay. It's there. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you obtain or see from the office of the Prosecution any similar sheet for code-names or index of names of intercepts with respect to your book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear so it's easier for you this is a code-name list for the VRS, the next document is 1085, I would just ask that you briefly look at that. Because I mentioned that that was the index of names on intercepts. So if you could just take a look at that so I can show that I was fair to you, even though you answered the question. It's coming up now, sir. And this is the index of names on intercepts that I was referring to. Did you ever, with Stefanie or anyone with -- at the office of the Prosecution, create an index of names for some of these codes that you recorded or others in your unit recorded in the book that we've discussed during your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I didn't. Although I did mention some of the coded names for which I knew the identity fully, and I think that in 1999 this was written down during one of the meetings. But those were the names of the people who had used these code-names throughout the war, and we were 100 per cent certain of their identity. If necessary, I can identify some of those names. I didn't really deal with this specifically, this was just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm interested to know too, so thank you for the invitation, and I will accept you on it. Who was Premijer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I think that Premijer was the communications centre of the 1st Zvornik Brigade. What they did was retransmit, that is to say if the connection was bad they would retransmit the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And one name that I'm interested in, who was Strsljen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I can't remember. I followed Premijer for a long period of time, almost throughout the entire war, so that's why I could remember that name. But as for Strsljen, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. In your book I noticed a couple words that I needed your assistance with. And I'll read them out in English, and hopefully -- I couldn't necessarily find them in the B/C/S language, but in the 13th and 14th of July, 1995, there is an entry there about war materiel. Do you remember what war materiel would have referenced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The best way is to show him the reference, I think, as opposed to his memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed. I'm sure Mr. Ostojic can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's on page -- on the English version, page 7, I think the same page that the Prosecutor was using with the witness, which would be on P2232, page 7. And according to at least the English version, this is conversations that were taken on the 14th of July, 1995, which is the same page my learned friend referred to. And it's in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It starts with, "On a frequency 293 at 2045." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I have the English version and I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, if the usher could hand him the original version and he can find it. It should be tabbed already since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we could see from what was on the ELMO is that I think that page is tabbed, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, so if you could look at the yellow tab when you were on your direct, I think it's the second yellow tab. But you could help, since you helped tab these, I think, maybe you could find the entry for the 14th of July and then it's three pages after that. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Could you please tell me again which intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's "On a frequency 293 at 2045." Did you find it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to let us place it on the ELMO and just point to that intercept so that we can maybe follow along, which is at frequency 293 at 2045. Okay. Now, can you read that sentence to us, please, because I have questions regarding three different -- four different points in that sentence, if you don't mind. Can you read it into the record for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: "Igman 1 - Lovac 1 and Lovac. Surround the forces with war equipment, reinforcement is arriving from the Main Staff. Mome's men are coming now." Most likely it says "Mome's."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is, do you know what was being referenced when they said "war equipment"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I suppose that he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought so, but I didn't want to be presumptuous. What are they talking about? What type of war equipment are they talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: We could only suppose at the time what kind of war equipment, most likely tanks, Pragas, personnel carriers, and other things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Other things like ammunition, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Naturally. Because without ammunition equipment means nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, this word "reinforcement" is coming, what is that? What is that? Can you describe that, tell me what you thought that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: It most likely means, I can't now go into the essence of what happened before and what happened after, but I can suppose that they believed that they did not have enough men, and they asked for reinforcement and this message had been sent and then they told them that new reinforcement was on its way from the Main Staff, and that there would be some additional people from Mome. I believe that it says "Mome" here. I don't know who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you able to capture or record, in the book that you have, any other reference to Main Staff regarding war equipment or reinforcement, other than this one entry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, the organisation of radio communication that we monitored was such that the words Main Staff and people's names were used infrequently. The case was quite different on radio relay communication. What was mentioned here was quite a rarity, such words as Main Staff, names of commanders, and so on, that was mentioned very seldom. Perhaps the people who worked on radio communication were not really interested in mentioning these names, because it was organised by somebody else, and they merely executed what they were told to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And then just one other word I wanted you to help clarify with me. The word "axis," do you know what that is, a-x-i-s?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: In the same intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, no, it was referenced in an intercept approximately 10 pages further on, and it's on page 20 of the English version and it should appear, sir. And I think with the Court's permission, you could take the book, approximately the 16th of July, 1995. If you go to the 17th of July, it's about a half a page above that. If the Court permits, I think he will. So again, if I can just repeat it to help you a little bit. If you find the entry of the 17th of July, it would be immediately preceding that, so before the 17th of July entry. You should have it tabbed because you discussed it a little bit, something before that, you talked about the yellow soil with my learned friend, about the negotiation with the opposite side. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes, I did find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, can we place it on the ELMO, please. And this is a conversation between Palma and Lovac 1, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you just read the first sentence up to the town Govedarica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: "We are negotiating with the opposite side to have them come out near Nezuk and then the stream to the left towards Zuta/zemlja. Palma Lovac 1, we have agreed that their access is going to be towards the stream. So that we liberate at Resnik and Govedarica."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what they're referring to when they say "axis" there, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I think that they were referring to the axis of movement of the part of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was leaving the encirclement in Srebrenica because this is the period after some agreement had been reached and that was the direction that they were supposed to take on their way to Nezuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That was approximately the 16th of July, at least according to your book, correct, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: This is when it was noted down, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever record or identify any of the participants in the conversation by their first name Ljubo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at the entry of the 14th of July, 1995, sir. And again, the Court, I'm sure, will permit for you to take the logbook and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It should be tabbed because I think it was used. So if I can direct your attention to the 14th of July, 1995. Intercept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Make sure that he's found it because he's still flipping through the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will show him where it is, approximately, with that as a guide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the corresponding English page number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In English, it's page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Have you found the entry of the 14th of July, 1995, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you can place it on the ELMO. Just point it to us so we can orientate ourselves. Great. Now, in our English version, it all comes in one page. They don't break it off. So it's the page immediately preceding that, I would like to discuss with you, which is the paragraph above or, in your case, the paragraph that is on the left-hand side of the book where the date, the 14th of July, 1995, appears. Do you see that? And it's really the second line from the bottom where you talk about Premijer and then you have this Strsljen and then in parentheses you see "Ljubo," close parentheses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Most likely since it's written in the parentheses I would say that it was mentioned in a previous conversation, so the operator knowing that this involved some Ljubo, put this information in parentheses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your meetings with the various investigators and those including Ms. Stefanie, did you ever discuss with them who this possibly could be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that this is not Ljubisa Beara but it's some other Ljubo that hopefully, during the course of this trial, will present that evidence. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I am not in the position to know whether this is the Ljubo or some other Ljubo, but I'm sure that some Ljubo was mentioned, since we have this information in parentheses. Nobody would write down something unless there was a reason for that. There was no need for us to do that. I wrote down in one of the intercepts that the conversation was not really audible, so the operator noted that down. He didn't try to invent anything, he just wrote down that it was barely audible. So I know that this involved some Ljubo, but I don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. My next topic, and really it's my last topic, in the period of mid-July 1995, you referenced many ambushes. Do you recall that in giving your testimony earlier today? I'm sure you do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Your question is not quite clear. What do you mean by ambushes? Whose ambushes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, for my first question, it's irrelevant whose ambushes, but in the documents that you have provided us, the word "ambush" appears several times.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, if it concerns this document, the one that we provided, then these ambushes were the ones organised by the members of the Serb forces in order to capture as many people as possible. People moving from Srebrenica to the free territory, moving through woods, streams and so on. So these are the ambushes. In addition to what I mentioned here, I also remember quite a number of conversations which mentioned things like summary executions, no need to keep them alive and things like that. Some of that information may even be found in the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll look for that, thank you. With respect to the ambushes just, sir, how many ambushes were there during the course of that three or five-day period? Again, mid-July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, this entire encirclement is something that I perceive as ambushes because it's not like the members of the Serb army were only in one position, no. They were in various posts and forward positions, so it could only be perceived as ambushes. And as for how many times it was mentioned, you can see it in the conversations. It was noted down by the operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to be unfair to you. As you sit here, sir, having reviewed your logbook in preparation for your testimony, given that you met with two investigators, testified in another case, as you sit here, do you know what your best recollection is as to how many ambushes were conducted in mid-July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I can't remember, as I have said to you. Because there was so much going on. And in my preparations for the testimony, I didn't really focus on ambushes. There were such cases, there were lots of them. In addition to what was noted down, I also remember that I heard great many such conversations and I was tasked with conveying this to the others. So in addition to the operator, I also had to convey it and I know that there were great many such cases, but I can't tell you how many were noted down in this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just one final question, if can ask you this, with the Court's permission. I know you state that there were a lot of them. You said there were a lot of them, specifically on line 25 of page 45. Does that mean to you more or less than seven?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Definitely more.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. I have Ms. Nikolic or Mr. Bourgon for Drago Nikolic. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you based on where you were in July of 1995. And my first question is I would ask that you confirm -- maybe it's better if we move in closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on the basis of your book, Witness, and the conversations that are reported in your notebook, it is my understanding that there was more than one network in operation at the time where these conversations were intercepted from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes, there were many networks, and on different frequency ranges, they were not all on the same device, and all on the same frequency range. They were some measures from 30 to 69 megahertz and radio connections from 130 to 160 megahertz. At that point in time, perhaps we had other equipment, but actually, we were focused only on those two: 30, 69, 95, and 140 to 170 megahertz. There were several networks too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and maybe some of my colleague here, just to define what is meant in general terms by a network, would you agree with me that a network can be defined as a number of stations using the same frequency to communicate together? Would that be very general and basic definition of what a network is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes, three or more stations. Two can be considered to be a radio route, three or more can be considered to be a network, if they were in a radio network and if they were using the same frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, Witness, that it is possible for any one station to be heard on more than one network?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes. Some, usually the communications persons, would get some kind of plan for the connections and then they would know if somebody else was working also who was not in their network. The device allows them to move into a different frequency and to hear somebody who was not part of their network. This is of course possible if technical conditions allow that. We're talking about frequency ranges. Within one frequency range you can hear it, sometimes you cannot go into a different range. Or better said, the equipment has to be of the same frequency range in order for them to be able to hear each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, this last question that I posed was more addressed or not so much in the technical sense, but more in the fact that it is something that can happen for one station to have access, and to participate in conversations on more than one network.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes, if the technical conditions permit. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that usually any given network would change frequency from time to time and that you would -- you could maybe access that same network but you would have to find it whenever that network would change the frequency used? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: It's like this: Each radio network has several frequencies, and they are changed from time to time. They can be changed in time periodically or at the request of an operator. So in a more quiet period when the traffic is not so busy, perhaps it could be a problem to find the network again. But when the traffic is pretty high then, really, it's not that difficult. We would perhaps need a minute or two to find this new frequency. When the traffic was heavy. When it was light there would have to be some kind of broadcast to be able to locate it. You could not locate it without a broadcast. During this key period it was not difficult to locate a new network or a new frequency. A lot of it was known, whether there was some kind of code indicating a shift to a new frequency, we knew all of those codes, and we would monitor that, we would write them down, and we would almost simultaneously move to the new frequency as the other participants in the network.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, going back, or moving from this question, if in your notebook you have frequency -- I just use one example, I could use any, and I see frequency 150.185. And that's a frequency that was used for a particular station at any given time. My question to you is, if I see the same frequency again in your notebook, it doesn't mean that the same station is using it, and actually that the same network is using it the second time around. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, from what I managed to understand of the question, it's like this: If we register one frequency and two, three or four participants are operating on that frequency and then we if we were to hear again in an hour on the same frequency some other participants, it can mean that they are from the same network or from the same frequency, or it can mean that somebody new has joined that frequency. But believe me, when you are really into the work, when you work with that, you learn a lot, you remember a lot of the modulations, the timbre of the voice of the person that is speaking. And then it's is not a problem for you to recognise whether it's this speaker or that speaker. Perhaps for you as a lawyer it is difficult for you to understand this, but at that time for us it was really not a problem at all to be able to tell who is who.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. My last question, did you at any point in time establish or make a sketch of all of the networks that were in operations and all the stations for each of the networks or basically did you ever draw a communications plan in use within the VRS army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Before the activities, I did this kind of work throughout the whole war, so before I did have plans with descriptions of specific units, this participant is this, this participant is like that and so on. As for this period, first of all, it would be very difficult to describe that during the period of combat actions around Srebrenica. It would be difficult to make these differences because all the participants went from one frequency to another, so in my view perhaps it -- there were no clearly defined radio networks. The participants had the possibility for the Premijer to tap into a different network, so it was very difficult to define specifically who was part of which network and who used what frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. I have on my list the Borovcanin team. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have into questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Stojanovic and Mr. Lazarevic. I have the Miletic team. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, General Miletic's Defence has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Petrusic. The Gvero Defence team have now announced that they have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That remains the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And finally we have the Pandurevic team. Mr. Haynes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Witness, it's right, isn't it, that you achieved some excellence in the field of electronic warfare?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, I assume that I did, if I may evaluate myself.
