utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean you did -- you did receive decoration for your service in that field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I did, and I am proud of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you were familiar, very familiar with the sort of devices that, if I may put it that way, that the opposition was using in communicating with one another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And there were basically two systems, weren't there, there was the RUP radio and the Motorola?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Each of those had a range of about 20 kilometres. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Perhaps on paper, but in practice, especially in Bosnia, which is of a hilly terrain, and the lay of the land, it could have been perhaps two kilometres. If it's open terrain then it could have been greater, but through translators or repeaters, it can be augmented, but actually in practice, the range is not as high as it is stated in theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've anticipated my next question. The other weakness of this communication system is that they can't communicate with one another. If you have a Motorola, you can only speak to somebody else with a Motorola and if you have an RUP, you can only speak to somebody else who has an RUP.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: In technical terms, yes. That is why we use the communications centres which had the RUPs and the Motorolas, so some sort of communication devices that could communicate with hand-held Motorolas. They were a little different, so if there was need to communicate, they were used to convey certain information from that network to the other network.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. So we have two situations in which two parties who might want to speak to one another have to speak through an intermediary or a series of intermediaries either because they are on either side of a hill or because they're using different radio systems.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And without going to specific examples, that is why we see in the book that you are showing us very often more than two correspondents to any different conversation. You can see three, four, up to seven correspondents in some of these conversations or summaries.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: That's how it is usually. Perhaps in a description of a conversation, you can have participants that took part, but often an information is repeated five, six or 10 times, until it reaches the end user for that information or perhaps an order is repeated several times for three or four units. You are not going to find that in the notebooks, because the operator who was transcribing that perhaps felt that there was no need for him to copy five times over the same material.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, one thing I want to ask you about, which I don't think you've dealt with, is as it were, the creation of the summary in the book. At site one, which is the only site I'm interested in, there were a number of operators, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as you've already told us, conversations, even these repetitive conversations where a message is relayed down the line, would often take place on different frequencies or even different systems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, as I understand the position, the operators wrote notes on pieces of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Those pieces of paper have been destroyed but the contents of those pieces of paper were summarised into the notebook you've referred to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: The contents were entered but I cannot state that everything was entered. We only sometimes heard parts of conversations but what was entered, that was it. We would hear the conversations and we would pass it on to the forward command post, and perhaps not everything was written down. What I am saying is that not everything that we heard was entered, but what is entered is that. It's part of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What I'm really seeing if you can help with is whether the entries in the notebook might have been or were indeed the product of several operators' notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: The material, yes, but the transcription itself, no. Perhaps it was just entered by one or two operators. The gathering of the material was the output of all of the operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So sitting here today, when you look at that book, in particular, some of the conversations you have -- some of the entries you've been referred to, what, in fact, you are looking at is a summary of a number of operators' notes of a number of different conversations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: It's most likely a summary. These are not verbatim conversations of everything that was said. It's just a kind of skeleton or a cross-section.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very helpful. I'm going to put this to you in terms. It's impossible, isn't it, now, looking at that book, to attribute any particular words to any particular speaker?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I cannot attribute anything to anyone. I am not going to mention the names. But according to the call signs, the secret names, that person is said to have stated something. At the beginning I already said that I cannot claim that such-and-such a person is personally such-and-such a person. It's not something that I can claim. But that such a participant stated such-and-such a thing, that is certain. There is very little room for mistakes during the entering of the data, because there were several operators there mostly, and they consulted one another and that kind of thing. Very often several operators would listen to the same conversation, perhaps one of them can mishear something, but the others would then correct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's not really the point I'm putting to you. Many of the passages you have been referred to and have looked at are summary, and they are the summary of perhaps three or four people who have spoken during the course of the creation of that summary. What I am suggesting to you is, looking at that summary, you can't tell us now who contributed what to that summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that's a misstatement of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't read his evidence as necessarily meaning what you have suggested now. If you look at page 60, lines 4, I cannot attribute anything to anyone. I'm not going to mention the names. But according to the call signs, you can -- beginning of it, it said I cannot claim that such-and-such a person is person such-and-such." Or page 59, on line 15. The material, yes, but the transcript itself, no. Perhaps it was just entered by one or two operators gathering of the material was the output of all the operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very well, Mr. President. I was trying to deal with the matters generally. I will have to deal with it by specific example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will not stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to move on from there, if I may. Now, in the organisation of any military operation, one of the things that the commander will do is to create what's called a plan of correspondence; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, one of the commander's assistants would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what is meant by that is that the call signs and radio frequencies and reserve radio frequencies to be used will be set out for the purposes of the operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it is. Code-names are designated for various units, frequencies that are going to be used, codes that are going to be used for certain places, certain locations and certain activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The sort of radio equipment that was in use, that you were monitoring here, has many, many different frequencies, doesn't it? Perhaps I should say channels, set channels.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Both terms are correct. And there can be many of them. We already mentioned RUP 12, 30, 69 and 95. They have about 800 channels. As for Motorola frequencies, there can be a tremendous number of channels and frequencies that can be used there. I should also mention that the entire frequency range from 140 to 170 megahertz is something that the receiver can scan within a minute. The entire range and whenever something comes up in that -- in that range, the scanner will pick it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In setting a plan of correspondence you would limit the number of reserve frequencies that were going to be used during the course of the operation, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: You mean myself or somebody who is drafting the communications plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm asking you the question borne of your experience as an electronic warfare office?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That is still vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It would be usual, wouldn't it, during the course of drafting a plan of correspondence for a military operation, to have, say, eight or nine pre-set channels that would be used and which those who were communicating with one another would move to, to avoid being detected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Probably. Each plan can have a number of frequencies, not necessarily just 10. It can have 15. Which presupposes that all of the participants know when to switch to another channel. But let me repeat it now: Given the amount of communications during that period of time, it was no problem for us at all to detect it. It took us a minute or two and we would find the same network again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not doubting that for a minute. In fact, I'm trying to agree with you in that suggestion. I think by the -- by the 14th of July you had located many, many of the channels that were being used by the forces that you were monitoring, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you had also discovered the call sign that they used to indicate that there was a need to shift channels and that call was "Sava" wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes. Then they would say "Sava" and then a certain number and then the participants would then know that they needed to switch to that particular frequency. This was done in order to prevent us from knowing that they were switching to another frequency so that we wouldn't go searching it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And one of the other things you'd identified was the commander, the chief of the operations, and you had done by the 14th of July, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to try and refresh your memory. I'd like to put the book from site one, that's P02231 in B/C/S, and 2232 in English, on to e-court. And I'd like the witness, please, to see page 6 in -- I'd like us to see page 6 in the English and the witness to see page 11 in the B/C/S. This is at the very top of the page in English. It's about halfway down in the B/C/S, and what you are looking for, Witness, is the phrase "Lovac 1, it's the chief. They were looking for him to come to the base." I'm told the screen needs to go up a bit for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps he could be directed to the original, as we can see, we didn't get a very good image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that can be done. And it should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's the page with the ERN number at the top 8951.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the original here. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, of course. About halfway down you should see an entry which in the English translation reads, "Lovac 1- it's the chief. They were looking for him to come to the base."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, that could be an assumption of one of the operators. Based on something, based on a previous intercept he identified him as commander or somebody addressed him as chief, and based on that he made this notation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My point is that that is an identification of Lovac 1 as being the chief of operations of the forces you were monitoring, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That does not reflect the evidence. It doesn't -- there is no where does it say "operations".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not going to -- I'm not going to argue this in front of the witness, but that's a disingenuous objection. Mr. McCloskey knows very well the subsequent evidence we will find out very well who this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would ask the witness to leave the room so we can respond to this attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Either leave the room or -- do you understand English? I'm asking you, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Are you happy if he removes his headphones, Mr. Haynes and Mr. McCloskey? Or do you want him out of the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we can very easily clear this up. Mr. Haynes and I have been chatting about this. I think he used an unfortunate word but I'm fine if he removes his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So Witness, could you kindly remove your headphones, please. And Mr. Haynes, do you want him out or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, no. There really is very little between us here. It was probably a loose question, but I don't think there will be any dispute who Lovac 1 was in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He is not a chief of operation though, this is a important military distinction. We can maybe do the stipulation right now, who he is and what the evidence will come through, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm happy with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course. Let's go into private session. Let's make it more complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Haynes and Mr. McCloskey, we've had -- we've heard from both of you what we needed to hear and what is important to hear. Given that, we are going to leave it entirely in your hands to rephrase the question, whichever way you think reflects your position. I mean, we have understood what the position according to the Prosecution is. The witness can put back his earphones. Headphones, sorry. Headphones. And -- Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sorry about that, Witness. It was probably all my fault, but we'll get back to some questions now. You would agree now, and -- that passage I showed you was on the 14th of July, that by the 14th of July you had identified virtually all of the frequencies in use by the forces you were monitoring and you had identified somebody whom you believed to be the chief of those forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to object, but the first part of that question I think the witness had answered that it was impossible to identify all the frequencies. So that's a misstatement. I don't think it was purposeful, but again -- and it's a two-part question which makes it harder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can answer the question. He can answer the question. Yes, go ahead. Witness, can you answer Mr. Haynes's question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I have said, and I was about to say when the Prosecutor interrupted me, it was impossible to identify and monitor everything. There are no technical possibilities to do that, because they could always use other networks or frequency ranges and we would normally do what we were ordered to do or what we could technically do, that we were capable of. And as I said earlier, it's very difficult to identify various code-names and call signals with full accuracy. Perhaps this was noted down because one of the operators heard it in one of the intercepts. To tell you the truth, I listened to this, and I did not reach a conclusion that Lovac 1 was a chief. And the term "chief" alone could mean a number of things. Chief of Staff or chief of something else. So I never reached that conclusion that you are mentioning now. Perhaps one of the operators noted it down because, based on the context on what was said, that's the conclusion that he drew. Or maybe this reflects some personal fears that he had. Maybe he feared his own chief and concluded that this person was in charge on the other side too. Let me repeat that it is very difficult to accurately identify, and I do not want to be held to what I said about the possible identities. And in another situation in a different type of communication, perhaps in radio relay communication, perhaps they mention names more often, so it's easier to identify people there. I hope that this explanation was good enough. If not, please let me know and I'll try to explain again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the extent to which you have familiarised yourself with the book from site one. But much of the monitoring of communications from site one concentrate on Lovac 1 and Lovac, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Most likely they were one of the most powerful or frequent participants. Because what is noted down here was definitely uttered. There were some other intercepts, some other communications that were established but not recorded or not recorded in this notebook. So the notebook reflects only a small number of conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean, we are agreed on this, that in that book, Lovac appears 82 times, and Lovac 1, 62 times. It looks like your operators were concentrating on monitoring his communications quite closely, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, I didn't count how many times they were mentioned. The job itself, the frequency itself, the communications and the content of communications was such that we focused on this. This was a long time ago, and it's hard for me to say that my reasoning went along these lines, I know this guy and I feel like listening on to him. But at the time they were probably the participants that interested us and we zoomed in on their network and followed them, monitored them. I'm sure that there were many other conversations on other frequencies that were also of interest to us, but we didn't monitor them because we were focusing on this particular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As you've said, not only did you monitor Lovac 1 very closely, you followed him every time that he moved frequency, I suggest to you. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, this kind of imposes itself. I told you that already. He switches the frequency, we go look for him, detect him, and monitor him again. Most likely they were mentioned more than others because we were interested in their conversations more than in another's. When scanning the frequency range, one comes across various conversations, including ones that were not relevant for that particular area, that are completely irrelevant, and we would not record them or note them down and try to detect their call signals, while neglecting what was of interest to us. That was the reasoning why we did what we did, and now it seems as though we focused only on Lovac 1 and Lovac 2, but that wasn't the case in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in that regard, some sort of indication that he was, and I will use as neutral a phrase as possible, an important commander or an important chief, would have made you double and redouble your efforts to make sure you captured every one of his communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Perhaps we didn't have to double our efforts. We simply monitored that network and that was it. We successfully found them again, whenever they changed frequencies, and the operators made certain assumptions about the importance of certain participants who were indeed important. It would be stupid for me to say now that these participants were not important for us when we monitored them closely. Now, as for doubling our efforts in order to monitor them, most likely we would have done it had there been other conversations in that frequency range that were not important to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to ask your view of this: Given the close monitoring of this particular radio user, would you think it conceivable that that person could have dictated a long report over the radio without you hearing it and making a note of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I don't know, to tell you the truth. Let me tell you something. I can't remember, this was quite a long time ago. And I'm not in the same line of work anymore. So I'm a bit rusty. I don't remember these things. But let me tell you what's important: Perhaps something could have escaped our attention because we were not experts who never missed anything. Also, perhaps that we registered some reports, but they are not included here. Because let me repeat again, there were many, many things that I cannot find going through the notebook. They were conversations that were recorded and their content was simply conveyed to the forward command post without recording them. And that is the problem, because had they been recorded, our job would have been easier, as would be yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I would just like you to have a look, please, at what is page 8 in the same exhibit in the English, page 13 in the B/C/S. And if you would prefer to look at the document on ELMO, the number at the top of the page on the physical exhibit is 8953.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I found it. What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm wrong about that. It's page 4 in the English, page 9 in the B/C/S, and the number at the top of the page on the physical exhibit is 8948. Have you found it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm looking at an entry that should be at the bottom of the page for you, which in the English reads, "L1 requested a vehicle to come and pick him up because Lovac needed to talk to him urgently. After that they sent a Peugeot car."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I don't see it on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It might be 8949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was the same page to which Mr. Ostojic had referred you before where there is the entry for the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The number at the top of the page is 8949, not 8948. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I remember well, it should be on the left side of your logbook. That's how Mr. Ostojic described it. How long will you be on this particular page, Mr. Haynes, because we need to have a break soon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I have got one or two questions about this page, then I want to return to something I was asking the witness about before and then I'm finished a topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Should we have the break now or what do you suggest? What do you prefer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Could I just finish this topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Did you find the relevant part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Firstly, can you confirm that, in this book, the use of the letter L and L1 is equivalent to the use of the words Lovac and Lovac 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I already mentioned that before and also in my previous testimony, that a large number of abbreviations was used. Just so as not to lose time, not to write out Lovac 1, Lovac 2 in full. In any other event these abbreviations were used. With other words, if you wanted to say testing the communications, then you would use these abbreviations just so that you do in the waste time rewriting the same phrases over and over again. Whenever, in the notebook, you find that there is an L or L1 participant, the -- that signified Lovac 1 and Lovac 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you also confirm that the accuracy of that particular entry, that Lovac 1 requested a vehicle to come and pick him up because Lovac needed to talk to him urgently and after that they sent a Peugeot car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I believe that it is accurate. I mean, I cannot be 100 per cent sure, but I believe that that is accurate. They sent a Peugeot. It means that from the rest of the conversation somebody informed him that a Peugeot was sent to pick him up. And so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would you take it from me that that was on the 13th of July? I'm sure we can agree that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, that was -- that was the sort of information that you were recording about Lovac 1 on the 13th of July. On the 14th you discovered or somebody discovered that he was the chief. I'll simply put this to you: After that discovery, you would have noted down, wouldn't you, if he had used his radio to dictate a combat report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. This has been asked before. We're going back over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's in a different context now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is in relation to combat reports now. And I think we can accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you remember the question or do you want me to repeat it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: There's no need to repeat it; it's already been said. The chief of Lovac 1, we've already said that I know what I said, and I think that's clear. There's no need to repeat myself. As for the combat reports, I am not informed about that. I don't know exactly what you mean. If you're thinking of the frequency of the conversations involving Lovac 1 and Lovac 2, we've already talked about that. But if you consider the conversations to be the same as combat reports, then that's all right. But as for any longer kind of reports, then I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll put it this way: On the 14th of July, after the information that led you to believe that Lovac 1 was the chief, would your operatives have been instructed to record and write down anything he said over the airwaves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Again, well, I hope that we resolved the issue with Lovac 1 and the chief. Secondly, they received instructions from me, what they would be monitoring. But if I was not there, I already mentioned the system that we used. Lovac and Lovac 1 themselves, in their conversations, the content of the conversations, forced us to monitor them and to stay with them. They wouldn't have forced us to do that if it was a false network because that is something that we very quickly established. We knew these were reliable pieces of information and naturally we monitored that. And we also monitored everyone else who was in their network and not only in their network, you will find in the notebook that there were also others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. McCloskey has been proven right because when you condense this answer, I don't see much difference from what the witness said from page 70, line 15 to page 71 line 18. It's more or less the same. Anyway, you are free to conclude on this part, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We can take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We will have a break of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I see from behind the column, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want to know what's happening with your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Good afternoon. I understand there is approximately 20 to 25 minutes left of cross-examination, that there is a short redirect and that Your Honours will issue a ruling so I wondered if I could release the witness. I don't think we'd get to more than a few minutes of his testimony. He's been waiting for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can release the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Witness, I've got three topics left to deal with you, and I'm going to take them as briefly as I can. I want to ask you about a couple of code-names that appear in the book from site one. And you've already referred to both of them. The first is the name Pavle, and that appears first of all at pages 13 and 14 in the English, and for your benefit, in the book it's page 8957 at the top, or page 17, B/C/S, on e-court. Have you found it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you should see the name Pavle linked there together with Vuk and Ikar and then lower down on its own.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes, I see the code-name Pavle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you can confirm that it appears on that page three times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I see it there as four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll stand corrected. And could you now go to page 17 in the English. That's on your book, Witness, is page 8960 at the top. Or page 20 in B/C/S e-court. It should be near the top of your page, Witness. And it's in a section that begins --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I've found it. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to read that over to yourself. I'll read it to you in the English. It says, "Palma asks, Lovac 1, that's L1, if the blue police could shift to the right and leave at 1000 hours. L1 gave them a message that they were going to set off at 1000 hours. At 0610 hours Lovac 1 asked Ikar to check with Pavle if they left as Lovac 1 ordered them to. Vuk told Pavle to speed up the insertion of the blue at the right wing and move on as soon as possible. Pavle has to make contact with me ASAP." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to take unfair advantage of you. We agree, that is the Prosecution and myself agree that those are the only references to Pavle in the whole of that book. So he's mentioned effectively in two conversations seven times. And I want to look at the text of that conversation that you're looking at now. Would you agree that from the text of that conversation that it appears that whoever Pavle is, he is somebody who takes orders from Lovac 1, Vuk and Palma?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, you can see from the conversation that Pavle is supposed to do something in compliance with an order from Lovac 1 and Palma.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And also Vuk tells him to speed up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that it appears whoever Pavle is, he is someone who is subordinate to those these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Well, you can conclude from this conversation that he is subordinate to Palma and Lovac 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you also conclude from the fact that he only appears twice in the whole of this book in two conversations, he's not a terribly significant operative for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I'm going to go back to the -- to what I said before. We were monitoring certain frequencies, I'm not going to say that Pavle was not important to us. At that moment everything was important to us, and I'm not going to say that this is the only conversation where this certain Pavle was mentioned. I don't know who it is, but the fact is that if you went through the notebook, I haven't really gone through it in detail for a long time in order to be able to refer to specific names, but if you went through it and that -- you say that's it, then it's possible that he has been mentioned that many times. But also, throughout the whole operations it is impossible that there were no other conversations where Pavle was mentioned, but we have just what is written here. And you can conclude on the basis of this conversation that he was receiving orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, one of the other persons mentioned in that particular conversation is Palma. Now, is Palma a code-name with which you were familiar before you embarked upon this particular operation from site one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I think that Palma was the command of the 1st Zvornik Brigade. Palma was used in radio relay communications. Here it's said, and you can connect it to that in some way, but again, in radio connections, the names and the secret codes are very difficult to link together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to show you some other passages to indicate that your operators seem to draw a distinction between Palma, as it was the organisation, and Palma, a person. I'm going to ask now that you be shown, please, page 18, English, e-court, page 21 B/C/S e-court, and for your purposes, Witness, that's 8961 at the top. Can you see it at 9.25, and again a little lower down, below 10.30, that the correspondent is said to be "Palma in person"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: "Palma in person" means that unit commanders addressed each other in person. If you say some unit it's not necessarily a person, but if you said "Palma in person" it would mean that that would be the commander of that unit. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. So your understanding of the codes, even before you were involved in this operation, would be that "Palma in person" would indicate the commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I assume that that was so, but I don't think you can state anything with certainty, but in all operations, that addition "in person" was something that referred to the unit commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would the contrary be true, that if the entry did not contain "in person" it would simply indicate that it was a communication from command headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: That would be that, yes. If you just mentioned the secret name, it could be that somebody from the centre of the brigade or the centre of the unit was conveying something, but if you say "in person" for the most part what was meant by that was the commander of that unit. Or the komandir, if it was a lower ranking unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I dare say you were aware of that -- at that time that the commander of the Zvornik Brigade was Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I know that certainly recently you've had occasion to hear his voice, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: No, I didn't. No. Even if I were to hear it now, you cannot really compare that to how it was then, and I've already said it was quite a long time ago, so I'm not in that environment anymore. I'm not doing that sort of work anymore. So I really don't think that I would be able to recognise the voice now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Please don't misunderstand the question, but during the course of your proofing for coming to give evidence here, you were played a tape, weren't you, by Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you were able to identify some of the people who were speaking on that tape. One of them was Semso Muminovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes, but it wasn't difficult to recognise his voice. He has a characteristic voice, so it was no problem at all to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And he was speaking on that tape to Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I know that not from this kind of work, not from radio reconnaissance. I know it. I was at some points in time next to Semso Muminovic when the negotiations were underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you next to him on both the 15th and the 16th of July when such conversations took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I said that I was not next to him all the time, but I was there for some of the time when the negotiations were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. How many conversations were you present at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: To be honest, I was doing other work at that time, but I was there two -- perhaps for two conversations, and I didn't really pay so much attention to that. It wasn't in my job description to monitor that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I understand that, but you now know, you probably knew then that one of them was being recorded. Was the other one recorded as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. The conclusion of the first -- in the first question --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's fine, I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's the case of putting two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You heard that tape this week. From the best of your recollection, was that a conversation you were present at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: There were more conversations probably. I cannot recall all the particulars of a conversation. And as I said, that's not what I would have been able to do. I mean, had that been the only thing since 1995 that I was supposed to remember, I would probably have remembered it. But that wasn't the only thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was there a tape recorder being used at either -- sorry. Was there a tape recorder being used at either of the conversations you were present at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I am not really aware of that, but perhaps there could have been a Dictaphone like the journalists would use. I did not record it, so -- myself, so I really don't know if there was some other recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The conversations you recall, were they on the same day or more than one day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I was there for the duration of one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so far as you were aware, did Semso Muminovic speak to any other member of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I never really discussed that topic with him. I know that when I would come to the forward command post, and if I wanted to see him, I was told that he was speaking with Pandurevic, and after that I never really spoke with him. I had no need to ask him who or if he spoke with somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Regardless of what you were told directly by Semso Muminovic, you have told us there were a number of people present. Did anybody else ever tell you that he spoke to anybody other than Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: To make it clear from the start, I was not at the command post then, the forward command post. Perhaps I came when that part of the conversation was going on. I wasn't there to see what Semso Muminovic was doing or to question any of those present at the forward command post, what Semso Muminovic was doing, whether he spoke with Vinko or this person or that person. I had my own assignments at the time, I completed them. This did happen at the time. I was a participant there, even though that did not occupy too much of my attention. So I don't know. I didn't ask anyone at the forward command post about it; I had no need to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, did you ever hear any suggestion that Semso Muminovic had spoken to somebody called Vukotic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I personally didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you turn your book, please, to page 8957? That's page 13 in the English. It's a passage you've looked at before. It's -- it should be about halfway down your page, maybe only a third of the way down, and it's the passage that begins, "Vuk- Lovac 1330 hours."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I found it. When I said that I didn't hear, what I meant, I didn't hear from anybody present. This conversation I read it later, but to tell you the truth, these negotiations were not within my scope of duties, and what is written down here was written down in order to record the thoughts and the position of the army of Republika Srpska. I personally wasn't interested in who talked to whom and so on. At that moment, I wasn't even paying attention to whether this was Vuk, this was Pandurevic. All I was interested in were the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Given what you know, leave aside what's in front of you, given what you know about what was going on over the period that you were at the forward command post, is it possible that in those entries where it is written "Vuk" should be written "Vinko"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Most likely this operator would not have written down "Vuk" without a reason. He must have been mentioned. They couldn't write Vinko at all, because operators were really not privy to the identity of a participant. Most likely this was mentioned earlier. In this case, the conversation was between Vuk and Lovac, a code-name was used, but I don't know anything about this code-name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just going down the page a little, you can see, can't you, from the -- what's written in the book, that the first conversation concerning Semso or Zukov was at 1330 hours that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And at 1410, that's 40 minutes later, an order was given to cease all activities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: It says here that a truce had been agreed, and that further firing should stop.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you mind repeating your last sentence, Witness, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: It says here that they agreed on a truce, following which a shell was fired and then they mention artillery Igman, and Igman 1, and then following that they asked for all further action to cease at 1410.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more thing on this point. In the tape recording you listened to with Mr. McCloskey, it's right, isn't it, that Semso Muminovic refers to Vinko Pandurevic by his first name, Vinko, and Vinko Pandurevic refers to Semso Muminovic by his nickname, Zukov?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Most likely that's how it is. This recording was made on Dictaphone, so other voices are heard as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How do you know the recording was made on a Dictaphone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I suppose so. Because nothing else could have been used. I don't think that a UHER was used, because there wasn't one there. There was also no computer at the forward command post, so there was nothing else but Dictaphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we now go, please, to page 19 in the English. For you, Witness, it's 8961 at the top. And it's page 21 in the B/C/S e-court. Have you got the page, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And to help you, we're looking at the very bottom of that page at the entry that's timed 11.40.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just so that it's in the record, it reads, "Igman 1 said that weapons are to be ready to fire at planned targets. During this period, user Sidro was not responding and everyone called him. They also fired their artillery at our weapons. At 1140 they seized some elements of our weapons but they did not fire because of the cease-fire." It appears from that at 1140 on what is the following day, the 16th of July, there is still a cease-fire in place or there is a cease-fire again in place from the previous day. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I can't remember now. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I don't think there is in evidence in the record that there was a cease-fire on the 15th. Perhaps I'm wrong, but I didn't see that. If I am, I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, what's your position on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I thought I had just elicited the answer in relation to page 13 that there was an order to cease all activities and the activities were stopped. It's at page 13 in the English. And the witness has just given the evidence that his understanding was that there had been a cessation of activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Would you like Mr. Haynes to repeat the question to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Looking at that entry for 1140, it appears that there was a cease-fire in existence at that time, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And on the question of interpretation of these summaries that we were dealing with earlier, can you help me as to what it means when it says "they also fired their artillery at our weapons"? Who is "they" and who is "our"? Can you tell one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I can't decipher this with great accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. That was my point earlier on. It's very difficult to because it's a summary of conversations that have been summarised for you by a number of people. That's the position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Based on this conversation it is clear that Igman 1, which must be somebody in charge of the artillery, conveyed that the weapons are to be prepared to fire at previously determined and planned targets. And then it says that participant Sidro did not respond, everybody called him in order to convey something to him, but they didn't manage to get in touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, would you just go over the page, please, because I'm going to try and finish with you today, if possible. To your page 8962. We're still on English page 19, and we will go over to page 20. And that's in the B/C/S, page 22 on e-court. Now, you read this passage earlier. It's the one that reads, "Palma in person for Lovac 1 in person." Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it goes on, "We are negotiating with the opposing side that they get out in the direction of Nezuk up the stream and up the left towards Zuti/zemlja." "Palma 1 to Lovac 1." This looks like a separate call. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by separate call.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, the participants, Palma and Lovac 1 are listed again. So it suggests that -- it's a separate call from the one previously we were reading.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it says, "We agreed that their axis is going to be towards the stream so that we liberate Resnik and Govedarica. We are going to open it there and once it passes we are returning to our old positions. It is about the withdrawal of our dead and you said that that was the BiH dead and wounded and the Chetniks received an order to shoot, if someone attempted to go into the depth of the territory and that message was at quarter past 1.00 in the afternoon. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that time, what you weren't asked to read by Mr. McCloskey, is the Chetniks received an order not to open fire while the men were going through. I would like, since you weren't asked this, your interpretation of that sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: No, this pertains to the same thing. Members, and I already said that members of the army of Republika Srpska had been given an order not to fire at Muslim forces unless the Muslim forces do that first. I have mentioned that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Witness, I had one or two other questions of you, but I see the time and I don't see there is any need to keep you here just to ask them, so I am not going to ask any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Do you think you can finish your redirect in two minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead. And I thank you so much, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, this RUP radio that you say was operated by the VRS that you were capturing communications from, did that have an encryption mode or cipher mode?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: RUP 12 is a device that has absolutely no encryption capability. There was another device, and those who are not familiar with the equipment could easily confuse them because they're almost identical. This one with encryption capability was called RUP 2/2K. It's a basically similar device, but it has an additional segment which enables encryption. So this additional segment enables the participants to have encrypted communication, something that cannot be detected with ordinary equipment. However, there were ways of getting around that, sometimes they would not use the encryption segment, and they would speak openly. Sometimes that happened. We would force them to stop using the encryption device, and to use the language that was intelligible to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the Motorola, was there any way to encrypt the Motorola?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: If simple Motorolas were used then, yes, there are so-called Motorolas with a scrambler that have the encryption capability. And they can be jammed. They used it seldom because other participants could not understand them, and they would not be able to communicate with other participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know from -- or did you have information from listening to these communications from the VRS and the Serb police how many men from the Serb army or police forces were killed before the corridor was opened on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know it's late, but I think it's beyond the scope -- I'm sorry. Beyond the scope of the cross, and if he wanted to ask that, he should have asked that possibly in his direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you have the same objection, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Quite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the tenor and the meaning of much of his cross was that his client opened this corridor out of some --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I don't think he ought to say any more in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think my point is clear, that there was some exculpatory...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our conclusion is that certain part of the cross-examination was broad enough to allow for the conclusion that this arises from it. So go ahead, Mr. McCloskey. And please try to bring your redirect to an end because we have already overstepped by five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have any information of how many young Serb men died before the corridor was opened on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-122
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I didn't have any reliable information. But I think that it wasn't a significant number because those people were not armed. This is my opinion. And I didn't have any specific information to this effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just wonder whether Mr. McCloskey would be good enough to clear up an answer the witness gave in redirect, namely, how it is that this witness and his operatives forced the Bosnian -- the army of the VRS to speak openly, because it's plain on his witness statement. I didn't cross-examine him about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we, not being technical people, how can you -- you said that there is the R -- RUP 2/2K, which had an encryption device segment, but however, you were in a position to force the VRS to stop using that encryption device, and to use the language that was intelligible. How could you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is how we did it: If, when scanning a frequency range, or if during the conversation they would mention that they are going into safe mode, then all we could hear were unintelligible signals. We couldn't hear any figures, names or anything like that. So whenever we came across such communication, we would jam them briefly with a powerful device. And this jamming would interrupt the signal so that the other person on the other end could not understand it either. In the majority of cases, throughout the war, based on my experience, the signalsman, since they have to pass the information across, would switch off the encryption device and talk openly. Whenever they tried to use such devices, there would be a serious miscommunication between them. And very often they would then speak openly about topics that should normally be encrypted. And the best way to force them to cease using encryption would be to jam their conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the same time, and please, Madam Registrar, you could communicate to Judge Antonetti the reason why we overstepped our minute. But that would also mean that they would be immediately aware that someone is monitoring that conversation. So it would be tantamount to going back to a situation or position where they would continue to be monitored. Would that not be a correct proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not necessarily. Because in the middle of the conversation they could not, or they could hardly realise that there was jamming, because they receive encrypted message. They don't hear audible human voice. And they could think that, yes, there is some interruption, but they do not necessarily have to conclude that it's due to jamming. It could be due to other problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We have to stop here. Witness, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony and I am thanking you on behalf of the Trial Chamber. I also wish you a safe journey back home. Our staff will attend to you. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. We will address the exhibits and we will give our ruling tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 9th day of March, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 25
